title: WHY DID JESUS SAY MOSES ALLOWED SOMETHING GOD NEVER INTENDED “FROM THE BEGINNING”?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS SAY MOSES ALLOWED SOMETHING GOD NEVER INTENDED “FROM THE BEGINNING”?
The disturbing words of Jesus about divorce, hardened hearts, and the difference between what God permits in a fallen world and what God designed before sin broke it.
There is a sentence from Jesus that can make a careful Bible reader stop.
Not because Jesus contradicts Scripture.
He doesn’t.
Not because Moses got God’s will wrong.
That is not what Jesus says either.
But because Jesus reveals something about the human heart that is uncomfortable enough to follow us home.
The Pharisees came to Jesus with a question about divorce.
On the surface, it sounded theological.
“Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause?”
But Jesus did something remarkable.
They wanted to debate the boundary of what was permitted.
Jesus took them back to what God intended.
He answered:
“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female...?”
Then Jesus brought them to Genesis—to creation, covenant, union, and the mysterious reality of two becoming one flesh.
And He concluded:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
That should have ended the conversation.
It didn’t.
Because they had another verse.
They asked Him, in essence:
Then why did Moses allow divorce?
And Jesus answered with words that still expose religious hearts today:
“Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so.”
Matthew 19:8.
Read that again.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
In Greek, Matthew records:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως
ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs
A natural rendering is:
“But from the beginning it has not been this way.”
There is the tension.
Moses permitted something.
Jesus says it was not so “from the beginning.”
So what happened?
Did God change His mind?
Did Moses lower God's standard without permission?
Was the Law of Moses flawed?

Or is Jesus showing us something much deeper about Scripture, sin, mercy, and the terrifying ability of human beings to become so hardened that divine legislation must sometimes address the devastation of a fallen world without pretending that devastation represents God's original design?
Because this conversation is about divorce.
But it is not only about divorce.
It is also about us.
We are remarkably skilled at asking:
“What am I allowed to do?”
when perhaps the more searching question is:
“What does the heart of God desire?”
And those are not always the same question.
The Pharisees appealed to Moses.
Jesus appealed to creation.
That distinction matters enormously.
Their question refers back to Deuteronomy 24:1–4, a passage involving a man who divorces his wife, gives her a certificate of divorce, and sends her away.
The Hebrew expression associated with that certificate is:
סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת
sefer keritut
Literally, a written document of cutting off or severance—a certificate of divorce.
But here is something crucial.
Deuteronomy 24 is often spoken about as though Moses were standing before Israel enthusiastically establishing divorce as God's beautiful ideal.
That misses the nature of the passage.
The text addresses an already broken situation.
A divorce has happened.
A certificate has been given.
A remarriage has occurred.
Then another separation takes place through divorce or death.
The legislation regulates what follows.
It does not present marital rupture as the creation ideal.
That is exactly why Jesus can acknowledge the Mosaic provision while simultaneously saying:
“From the beginning it was not so.”
Moses was dealing with humanity east of Eden.
Jesus takes His listeners back before Eden shattered.
Back before betrayal.
Back before domination.
Back before abandonment.
Back before lust.
Back before manipulation.
Back before men and women learned how to wound the people they once promised to cherish.
Back to Genesis.
“Male and female he created them.”
Then:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24 contains the Hebrew:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vehayu levasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
One flesh.
Not disposable flesh.
Not temporary flesh.
Not “until someone more exciting comes along” flesh.
One flesh.
Jesus therefore refuses to allow a debate over legal permission to obscure the sacredness of God's design.
But then He identifies the disease underneath the concession.
Hardness of heart.
Matthew uses:
σκληροκαρδία
sklērokardia
The word combines the idea of hardness with the heart.
It is where we get the concept behind the English word “sclerocardia.”
Jesus says:
πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν
pros tēn sklērokardian hymōn
“Because of your hardness of heart...”
And suddenly this passage becomes frighteningly personal.
Because hardened hearts did not disappear when the Pharisees walked away.
We still know how to harden ours.
We know how to stop listening.
How to justify what once convicted us.
How to collect Bible verses that protect the decision we have already made.
How to ask how close we can walk to sin without technically crossing the line.
How to turn commandments into loopholes.
How to call bitterness “discernment.”
How to call lust “a weakness.”
How to call pride “standards.”
How to call unforgiveness “boundaries” when what we actually mean is that we secretly want someone to keep paying forever.
How to call compromise “freedom.”
How to ask God to approve what we have never truly surrendered to Him.
And this is where Jesus refuses to play our game.
We ask:
“How far can I go?”
Jesus asks:
“What happened to your heart?”
We ask:
“Is there a verse that permits this?”
Jesus asks:
“Does this reflect what God intended?”
We ask:
“Can I technically justify myself?”
Jesus reaches beneath the argument and touches the wound.
Hardness of heart.
That does not mean every divorce happens because one innocent person woke up with a hardened heart and decided to destroy a marriage.
Scripture is more sober than simplistic blame.

Marriage can become the scene of grievous sin, betrayal, abandonment, coercion, violence, and profound human suffering. Jesus Himself speaks further about sexual immorality in Matthew 19:9, and Paul addresses abandonment by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7:15. Christians have disagreed over some details of how these passages should be applied, and faithful interpretation should acknowledge those debates rather than pretending every difficult case is identical.
But none of that changes Jesus' central movement in Matthew 19.
He moves from permission to purpose.
From Deuteronomy back to Genesis.
From regulation in a fallen world back to creation before the fall.
From the certificate in someone's hand to the hardness inside someone's heart.
And perhaps that is why this passage reaches much farther than marriage.
Because sometimes God regulates human brokenness without calling brokenness good.
There is a profound difference between God's holy design and provisions given within a world already ravaged by sin.
Fail to understand that, and we may confuse concession with celebration.
Regulation with endorsement.
Permission with perfection.
And then we may begin constructing our Christianity around the lowest boundary we believe we can technically survive.
But Jesus did not die merely to make us experts at locating loopholes.
He came to make us new.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not fundamentally:
“How much of my old life can I keep while still getting into heaven?”
It is:
“Jesus Christ gave Himself for me. What remains that I have not surrendered?”
And maybe that sentence makes you uncomfortable.
Good.
Stay there for a moment.
Because there are places inside us where we desperately want Moses' certificate when Jesus is asking about our heart.
There are relationships where we would rather prove ourselves right than become Christlike.
There are private habits we keep negotiating.
Secret messages.
Hidden resentment.
Pornography erased from browser histories but not surrendered at the cross.
Emotional affairs renamed “friendship.”
Greed renamed ambition.
Gossip disguised as a prayer request.
A marriage slowly dying because two wounded people have become more committed to winning than forgiving.
A faith slowly dying because someone learned how to look Christian without remaining close to Christ.
Nobody else sees it.
But Jesus does.
And here comes the scandal.
He sees it...
and still calls you toward Himself.
That is grace.
Not grace that tells sin it doesn't matter.
Grace that says sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
Not grace that lowers God's holiness until our rebellion becomes comfortable.
Grace that meets guilty people where they actually are and refuses to leave them there.
At the cross, we discover something far greater than permission.
We discover redemption.
Jesus did not come merely to answer the Pharisees' legal puzzle.
He came ultimately to deal with the hardened human heart itself.
The prophets had already pointed toward God's answer.
Through Ezekiel, God promised:
“I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.”
A heart of stone.
That sounds painfully close to the problem Jesus exposed.
And the Gospel announces that our deepest need cannot be solved by becoming cleverer religious lawyers.
We need mercy.
We need cleansing.
We need regeneration.
We need Christ.
We need hearts that can love what God loves again.
Maybe you are reading this after a divorce.
Maybe you caused tremendous damage.
Maybe someone else's sin devastated you.
Maybe you fought for your marriage until you had nothing left.
Maybe your story contains adultery.
Maybe it contains abandonment.
Maybe you carry regret over decisions you would give almost anything to reverse.
Maybe you have remarried and still wonder whether God sees you primarily through the worst chapter of your life.
Hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that your past was insignificant.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is greater than your past.
Repentance does not rewrite history by pretending nothing happened.
Jesus rewrites what history gets to become.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The woman caught in adultery was dragged publicly into shame.
Again and again, Scripture introduces us to people whose stories looked ruined.
Then Jesus entered them.
And whenever Christ enters a ruined story, sin does not suddenly become righteousness.
Something better happens.
Sinners can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come into the light.
The guilty can repent.
The wounded can begin healing.
The enslaved can become free.
The dead can live.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Because grace is greater.
Not cheap grace.
Not sentimental grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Cross-shaped grace.
Grace that forgives and transforms.
Grace that can look directly at the wreckage and still say:
“This does not have to be your final chapter.”
And perhaps this is the question Jesus' words leave burning inside us:
Have I been searching Scripture to surrender to God... or searching Scripture for permission to avoid surrender?
That question can hurt.
Let it.
Sometimes conviction is mercy knocking before destruction kicks the door down.
Maybe your issue is not divorce.
Maybe it is the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is what happens on your phone after midnight.
Maybe it is the bitterness you rehearse every morning.
Maybe it is the apology you refuse to give.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe you have become spiritually numb.
You still attend church.
You still know the songs.
You can still quote Scripture.
You can still say “God is good.”
But privately, something has become hard.
And the frightening thing about a hardened heart is that eventually it can stop feeling hard.
Sin begins feeling normal.
Conviction begins feeling irritating.
Repentance begins sounding extreme.
Obedience begins looking unreasonable.
Then one day we find ourselves asking exactly the kind of question Jesus' opponents asked:
“But am I allowed?”
When the King who rescued us is asking:
“Will you trust Me?”
There is no loophole that can heal your soul.
But there is a Savior who can.
His name is Jesus Christ.
Be honest.
Not because typing those words saves you.
Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need Him is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building.
Let other believers know that behind the profile picture is a human being who needs grace.
Someone reading silently may need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Not as a religious performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
But sharing biblical truth can genuinely become one small way of pointing someone toward Jesus.
Someone quietly preparing to walk away.
Someone hiding an affair.
Someone drowning in shame after a divorce.
Someone convinced that the worst thing they ever did permanently disqualified them from grace.
Someone who will never search for a sermon...
but might stop for an article you shared.
Am I seeking God's heart—or merely seeking permission?
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who has questions Christians sometimes seem afraid to discuss.

Supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful act of generosity when it is freely given from love for God and neighbor. The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
And there is something else we want believers to know about.
But whether you ever give us a cent or not...
Do not leave Jesus standing at the edge of the one room in your heart you refuse to unlock.
Because Matthew 19 is not merely an ancient argument about Moses.
It is a mirror.
Moses dealt with what hardened hearts had produced.
Jesus pointed back to what God intended.
And through the Gospel, Christ does something even more astonishing:
He takes hardened hearts and makes them new.
So stop asking only:
“What can I get away with?”
Ask:
“Jesus, what would You have me become?”
Bring Him the marriage.
Bring Him the divorce.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the certificate.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the consequences you cannot erase.
Bring Him the heart that does not feel anything anymore.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek forgiveness where forgiveness is needed.
Make restitution where it is possible and appropriate.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where circumstances require it.
And trust the crucified and risen Christ with the chapter you thought had permanently defined you.
Because the most astonishing thing about Jesus is not that He teaches us how things were “from the beginning.”
It is that through Him, broken people can receive something they could never manufacture for themselves:
a new beginning.
Because somewhere between “Moses allowed” and “from the beginning”, Jesus exposed the tragedy of the hardened human heart.
And somewhere between our scandal and His cross...
grace wrote another ending.
The chapter you are ashamed to reread may become the very page where someone else discovers that Jesus still rewrites lives.
